noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand the biological consequences of smoking in relation to the lungs and the circulatory system, including coronary heart disease

primer.text: Cigarette smoke is a chemical assault on two systems at once. Nicotine, carbon monoxide and tar each have a separate route of damage — vessels, blood chemistry and lung tissue — and the lung diseases they grow, chronic bronchitis and emphysema, dismantle the exchange surface itself.

lessons.title: Three Chemicals, Three Attack Routes
lessons.opening: Nicotine narrows blood vessels and speeds the heart, pushing blood pressure up and clot risk with it. Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin irreversibly, shrinking the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity and forcing the breathing and circulation to work harder. Tar is a carcinogen that also feeds chronic obstructive pulmonary disease — chronic bronchitis and emphysema together.
keyPoints: Nicotine narrows vessels, raises heart rate and blood pressure, and promotes clots.
Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin irreversibly, cutting oxygen capacity.
With less oxygen carried, breathing must quicken and deepen to compensate.
The heart pumps faster too, raising coronary heart disease and stroke risk.
Tar is a carcinogen and contributes to COPD: chronic bronchitis plus emphysema.

low.restatement: Each smoke chemical has its own target: vessels, blood cargo, or tissue.
low.analogy: Three intruders through one door — one jams the pipes, one steals the delivery vans, one burns the warehouse.
low.examPointer: Match chemical to consequence; mixed-up lists cost the marks.

medium.restatement: Less oxygen cargo forces the whole transport system to speed up.
medium.analogy: A fleet with stolen vans: the rest must run more trips, wearing the roads faster.
medium.examPointer: Use irreversible when describing carbon monoxide's binding — it is the specification's word.

check.stem: Which smoke component binds irreversibly to haemoglobin?

options.explanation: That binding is carbon monoxide's defining harm.
Nicotine acts on vessels and heart rate.
Tar is the carcinogen and mucus driver.
Carbon dioxide is a metabolic waste, not a smoke component here.

check.stem: What does nicotine do to blood vessels?

options.text: It narrows them, raising blood pressure
options.explanation: Narrowed vessels and a faster heart push pressure up.
The effect is constriction, not widening.
Nothing dissolves; constriction is the mechanism.
Vascular action is nicotine's headline effect.

check.stem: Why must a smoker breathe faster and deeper?

options.text: Because carbon monoxide has cut the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity
options.explanation: Less capacity per litre demands more litres per minute.

options.text: Because tar blocks the alveoli completely
options.explanation: Tar's damage builds over years, not as the direct breathing driver.

options.text: Because nicotine numbs the breathing muscles
options.explanation: No numbing is described.

options.text: Because smoke fills the lungs physically
options.explanation: The driver is blood chemistry, not blockage.

check.stem: Which disease pair does COPD name?

options.explanation: COPD is the combined diagnosis of those two.
Asthma is not in this pairing.
Heart attack belongs to the cardiovascular story.
Cancer risk is separate from the COPD naming.

check.stem: How does carbon monoxide raise coronary heart disease risk?

options.text: Through the compensatory faster pumping, which raises blood pressure and strains the arteries
options.explanation: The risk rides on the compensation, not on direct poisoning.
Nothing dissolves artery walls here.

options.text: By binding to the heart muscle
options.explanation: It binds haemoglobin, not the heart.

options.text: It does not raise the risk at all
options.explanation: The raised pressure and strain raise it.

check.stem: Name the three harmful chemicals in cigarette smoke named here.
State two cardiovascular consequences of smoking.
check.modelAnswer: Raised blood pressure and increased risk of coronary heart disease and stroke.

check.stem: Explain why the phrase irreversible binding makes carbon monoxide especially dangerous.
check.modelAnswer: Because each bound haemoglobin molecule is permanently out of service — no reaction can free it — so the oxygen deficit accumulates with every cigarette and the body can only compensate by working the breathing and circulation harder.

check.stem: A smoker's blood test shows reduced oxygen carriage. Trace the full chain to their raised heart-disease risk.
check.modelAnswer: Carbon monoxide occupies haemoglobin irreversibly, so less oxygen travels per litre; breathing deepens and quickens to compensate, and the heart pumps faster, which raises blood pressure, encourages clot formation and strains the coronary arteries — the chain from smoke to heart disease.

lessons.title: Bronchitis and Emphysema
sourceHeadings: Diseases of the gas exchange system linked to smoking
lessons.opening: Tar stimulates the airways' mucus glands to enlarge and overproduce; the mucus pools, blocks the smallest bronchioles and invites infection, while the cilia that should sweep it out are damaged and stop beating. The smoker's cough is the manual workaround. Frequent infections then summon phagocytes whose elastase digests the alveoli's elastic fibres — the alveoli lose their spring, burst, and the exchange surface shrinks.
keyPoints: Tar enlarges goblet cells and mucus glands, producing excess mucus.
Damaged cilia cannot sweep the mucus away, so it pools and breeds infection.
The smoker's cough is the attempt to shift the mucus manually.
Phagocytes responding to infection release elastase that digests alveolar elastic fibres.
Burst alveoli shrink the exchange surface, leaving sufferers breathless.

low.restatement: Mucus pools because the sweepers are broken; then the alveoli's springs are cut.
low.analogy: A cleaning crew on strike while the mess grows — then demolition of the storage shelves.
low.examPointer: Link tar to mucus to infection to elastase to lost surface — the full disease chain.

medium.restatement: Broken sweepers, then broken springs — bronchitis then emphysema.
medium.analogy: A escalator whose brushes fail, then whose steps crack: passengers pile up, capacity vanishes.
medium.examPointer: Order the chain correctly in answers; chronology carries the logic marks.

options.text: Tar, which enlarges the goblet cells and mucus glands
options.explanation: Tar is the chemical driver of the mucus flood.
Nicotine's targets are vessels and heart rate.
No such mechanism exists.
The cough responds to mucus; it does not create it.

check.stem: Why does mucus accumulate in a smoker's airways?

options.text: Because the cilia that sweep it are damaged and stop beating
options.explanation: Broken sweepers let the pool grow.

options.text: Because mucus production stops while drainage continues
options.explanation: Production rises while drainage fails — the worst combination.
They block, not widen.
No evaporation route is described.

check.stem: What role do phagocytes play in emphysema?

options.text: They release elastase that digests the alveoli's elastic fibres
options.explanation: The infection-fighting cells cause the structural damage.
They digest them; nothing repairs them.
Goblet cells make mucus; phagocytes bring elastase.

options.text: They carry oxygen to damaged tissue
options.explanation: Oxygen carriage is red cells' job.

check.stem: What happens to the alveoli once their elastic fibres are digested?

options.text: They become less elastic, cannot stretch, and many burst
options.explanation: Loss of spring ends in structural collapse.
No regrowth occurs.
They rupture rather than narrow.
Nothing hardens into bone here.

check.stem: Why do emphysema patients become breathless?

options.text: Because the burst alveoli have shrunk the surface area available for gas exchange
options.explanation: Less area means less oxygen transferred per breath.
Heart change is not the stated mechanism.
Mucus belongs to the bronchitis half of the story.
Thickening is not described.

check.stem: Name the two diseases of the gas exchange surface that occur together in COPD.
State the enzyme that digests alveolar elastic fibres.
check.modelAnswer: Elastase, released by phagocytes entering the lungs.

check.stem: Explain why a smoker's cough develops.
check.modelAnswer: Because tar-driven mucus pools in airways whose cilia are too damaged to sweep it out, so coughing is the only remaining way to move the mucus — the body's manual replacement for the broken conveyor.

check.stem: Explain why emphysema damage cannot be reversed by quitting alone.
check.modelAnswer: Because the burst alveoli are structurally gone — no regrowth replaces the lost exchange surface; quitting removes the ongoing assault but cannot rebuild the area already destroyed, which is why severe sufferers need supplemental oxygen for life.

glossary.definition: A chemical that raises the chance of cancer developing; tar is one.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: chronic bronchitis and emphysema occurring together.
The enzyme phagocytes release, digesting the elastic fibres of the alveoli.
The beating hairs that sweep mucus upwards out of healthy airways.
